Just wondering. I'm trying to decide between HMO or PPO + CDHP. My husband has cancer and will need a major surgery soon. I'm thinking PPO is better. I have never dealt with a CDHP before. Thoughts? (Also, damn does our current system suck....)
What has been your experience with CDHP (Consumer Driven Health) plans?

I've been on several and have also passed on several for a more traditional PPO. The thing you have to remember about a CDHP is that you must take an active role in your health spending. You can not just let the insurance plan take care of it. This is especially important with prescriptions. CVS and Walgreens charge much, much more for prescriptions. Now, it's not just inflating the price. CVS has been a full service pharmacy for me, keeping track of interactions, auto-refill service, notifications when prescriptions are ready. But then, I'm on a PPO- I don't see the underlying cost. If I were on a CDHP, I might go to Wal-Mart, which charges very little. Don't know about the service, but it's Wal-Mart.

My husband has cancer and will need a major surgery soon.

First, very sorry to hear. That sucks.

Believe it or not, CDHPs can be pretty awesome for major health events. Or not. You need to run the numbers. IME, hospitals will work with you on the higher deductible, but keep in mind that threshold gets passed, everything is 100% covered- at least in all the plans I've seen. As opposed to a PPO, which will often vary wildly in how much of a percentage gets paid.

CDHPs are a lot of work. However, if you take the time to figure out if the reduced premium gives you a net benefit- and with major health issues they often do- then you can see which type of plan offers you the most for your money. They're usually good for very healthy people or very sick people. Very healthy because of the lower premiums you pay. Very sick because you get to the point where you don't pay anything anymore faster than you will a traditional plan. CDHPs have also never had an in/out of network thing IME. This could become important to you. Cancer treatment can also lead to mental health treatment- which is a good thing and not a sign of weakness in anyone. However, I've seen a trend of psychologists and psychiatrists either seriously limiting the insurance they take or simply not being in network anywhere. This is a bigger deal with a PPO than an HMO.

Also keep in mind that prescriptions count toward your overall deductible. Since cancer treatment tends to come with a lot of drugs, you'll get to the "I don't have to pay anymore" threshold that much faster.

HTH
